newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE-Brazil has "caubois" just like U.S..
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Brazil has "caubois" just like U.S..

text.p: They come in their hundreds of thousands, wearing Stetsons, whooping and blasting the music of Kenny Rogers from their pick-up trucks.

Every year, Brazil's growing ranks of "caubois" converge in dusty traffic jams on this otherwise sleepy town in Sao Paulo state's fertile sugarcane and orange belt for 10 days of raucous rodeo competition and Wild West fun.

Barretos is the highlight of Brazil's 1,200 annual rodeos and the place to be seen for the suddenly fashionable world of "country" culture. "Until a few years ago rodeo was considered vulgar. Now it's chic," beamed festival organiser Emilio Carlos dos Santos.

In the normally European-oriented city of Sao Paulo, smart-set teenagers step expertly in U.S. Deep South-style line dances and sing country hits in word-perfect English. Even Brazil's popular soap operas have gone country with "King of Cattle," a racy tale of a millionaire rancher who falls in love with a beautiful but landless peasant woman.

"We all grew up watching Bonanza. Who never wanted to be the Lonesome Cowboy as a kid?" asked director Tania Lamarca, whose film "Buena Sorte" -- "Brazil's first country movie" -- is due for release in November.

The Barretos festival grew from humble origins. In the 1950s, teams of cattle-drivers began bringing their herds from deep in the interior to the town's refrigerated abattoir. They celebrated the end of their long trek with dare-devil competitions of equestrian skill.

In 1955, a local bachelors club decided to turn their exploits into a festival. This year, the Barretos International Rodeo attracted an estimated 1.1 million visitors to the purpose-built Cowboy Park, making it the second largest rodeo event in the world, after Calgary in Canada, organisers said.

For 10 hot days and nights in August, farmers in designer jeans and boots mixed with drunks, clutching the black Virgin Mary that is the patron saint of farmworkers. An old man produced a bellowing rendition of The Beatles' "Hey Jude" on a hollowed bull's horn as crowds milled around bars and stalls hawking everything from whips to chewing tobacco.

But the real action in Barretos was in a horseshoe-shaped, 35,000-seat stadium where, beneath the billboards of corporate sponsors, cowboys from Brazil and beyond were thrown one after another from evil-looking bulls or snorting, bucking broncos.

"They had to virtually carry me out of the ring," said Art Watson from California, on his first painful trip to Brazil as a professional bullrider. Brazilian bulls were altogether a more vicious breed than those on the North American circuit, and more wily at getting a man in the dirt, he concluded.

Local cowboy Genival Pereira Queiroz knows only too well the tricks of the local bulls, which are crossbreeds of strong European cattle and the quickfooted, humpbacked nilori breed from India. He takes medication daily to avoid the blackouts that a hoof to the head in 1993 still give him.
"It's that combination of power and agility that gets the gringos," he said.

On semi-finals night, the packed stands were a sea of white Stetson cowboy hats, bobbing in time with short, loud blasts of rock 'n roll anthems. The crowd went wild when rodeo commentator Asa Branca, known as White Wing, landed in a cloud of red dust in a helicopter.

The only moment of calm came with a half-time tribute to three recent departures to the great rodeo in the sky. Giant, beef-fed men, their hats clasped to their chests, shed silent tears for one of the deceased, a much-loved millionaire killed this year when his car struck a horse.

In the invitation-only box of a major Brazilian beer company, sponsors and media executives, arm-in-arm with models in frilly tops and knee-high boots, marvelled at the cash-generating potential of the new showbusiness phenomenom.
"Look at those fans, their cars, their expensive clothes. There's a lot of purchasing power out there," one gushed.

Tatiana Giatti, head of Brazil programming for Nashville-based Country Music Television (CMT), a kind of country MTV, said the channel had quadrupled its original first-year target of 100,000 subscribers in Brazil.

"Latin America is our market of gold," she said, toasting CMT's first live coverage of the Barretos rodeo. "Brazilians have always identified themselves with America, with Coca-Cola, with jeans. It's a very easy market for us to win."

Just outside the park, however, Brazil's other country lifestyle was on view for all to see as shabbily dressed rural workers trundled by in the back of rickety trucks after a day's work in the never-ending sugarcane fields. "Poor people don't go to the festival," said Emerson Adriano Coradini, a 23-year-old farmhand steering his horse through tall cane to check on his boss's cattle. "We don't have the money."
Brazil has one of the world's most unequal land distributions. Eighty percent of arable land belongs to ten percent of landowners. This year, 33 people have died in clashes over land.
